To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we developed a novel concept of molecular motors that self assemble into responsive supramolecules in water, and that the dynamic function of the motor units in the supramolecules can be reversibly switched by light.
we have designed and synthesized an amphiphilic, photo-responsive molecular motor, which self-assembles into responsive supramolecules in water.

the novel concept of amphphilic molecular motors that assemble into responsive supramolcular nanotubes in aqueous media is introduced, and the function of the molecular motors in supramolecular assemblies is studied by UV-vis spectroscopy and cryogenic TEM.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design and synthesis of novel molecular systems with dynamic functions and the study of the self-assembly of these molecular building blocks into complex supramolecular systems.
the development of molecular motors for use in aqueous solution.
the development of new concepts in the field of dynamic self-assembly in water.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the molecular rotary motor has been shown to self-assemble in water and that it retains its function in the supramolecular system.

the combination of the supramolecular self-assembly of amphiphilics with the dynamic properties of molecular motors allows to create a new type of dynamic supramolecular systems with a high degree of control over the self-assembly and the dynamics of the individual molecular motor units.

this work presents the first example of molecular rotary motors that self-assembles in an aqueous environment and that the supramolecular nanosystem is able to undergo reversible reorganization upon light irradiation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we were able to develop an artificial molecular motor that is able to perform its rotary function in aqueous media.
the molecular motors are able to self-assemble in water, the dynamic function of the motors is retained, and the supramolecular structures are responsive to the light.
we developed the first molecular motor that is able to self-assemble in water and that can be reversibly triggered by light to undergo a complete rotation cycle.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the combination of a photoresponsive azobenzene moiety and the self-assembly of a supramolecular system is an effective strategy for the design of dynamic nanosystems that can respond to external stimuli.
the self-assembled nanotube structures can undergo reversible photoinduced structural changes, i.e. they can reversibly change between distinct well-defined nanotube structures.
the combination of molecular motor units with self-assembled supramolecular systems in water is a powerful tool for designing responsive nanosystems with complex functionality.
